hey provide long-term protection

eat the invader
process it and display the fragments on it's surface using the MHC molecules
present the antigen to lymphocytes (T-cells and B-cells)

MHC molecules

they help activate the B-cells;
they eat the invader, process it, and display fragments on their surface to alert lymphocytes.

because the germs are hiding behind the cells and antibodies can't reach them, that's why T-cells are trained to reach them

Intracellular organisms (germs hiding inside cells, especially viruses)
Parasites
tumor cells
foreign cells

A large number of T-cell subpopulations and complex interactions between them.

ch2Flashcard

What are serological reactions used for?

To detect antibodies in a patient's serum
or to identify unknown microorganisms They rely on observable antigen-antibody reactions
"and allow quantitation (titration) of antibody".

ch2Flashcard

What is the immunological basis of vaccination?

Vaccination exploits the primary → secondary → booster pattern. A "practice run" is given so that when the real pathogen appears, the fast and strong secondary response kicks in immediately.

ch2Flashcard

After how many exposures/injections are maximum antibody levels usually reached?

After 3–5 exposures/injections.

ch2Flashcard

Describe the timeline and features of the secondary immune response

Lag period: only 2–3 days.
Antibody levels shoot up rapidly to a much higher peak than primary
Levels decrease over a much longer period, stabilising at a protective level.
Main antibody: IgG (class switching has occurred).

ch2Flashcard

Describe the timeline of the primary immune response.

Lag period: up to several days
Detectable antibodies: after 5–10 days
Peak: at about 3 weeks, then levels drop
Main antibody: IgM first, then switches to IgG.

ch2Flashcard

IgG, IgA, and IgM.
